[score-axis-sensitivity] I built all 12 graphs from the available corpus (archy's own src/ plus the 11 cached bench repos in bench/replay_cache/: click, datasette, fastapi, flask, httpx, mkdocs, pydantic, requests, rich, scrapy, starlette), computed compute_score on each, and ran three measurements per axis: (1) local sensitivity d(overall)/d(axis) at the actual baseline, verified numerically (eps=1e-4) to match the analytic form for a plain geometric mean, overall/(5*axis); (2) full-range leverage (overall delta when an axis is swept 0.01->1.0 with others held at baseline); (3) the doc's own metric, cross-project Pearson r(axis, overall). Headline: the aggregation is an EQUAL-weight geometric mean (overall = (mod*acy*dep*eq*cpx)**0.2), so no axis is structurally privileged; local sensitivity is purely a function of each axis's current value. Measured local-sensitivity ranking is equality (0.376) > depth (0.225) > modularity (0.216) > complexity (0.139) > acyclicity (0.133). This directly contradicts the SCORING.md claim that "depth barely moves the score / depth optimization is essentially toothless": depth is the SECOND most locally influential axis, ~1.7x more sensitive than acyclicity and complexity, which the doc credits with "non-trivial leverage." The doc's low-|r| evidence for depth is an artifact of low cross-project variance, not low sensitivity; and modularity has even lower cross-project |r| (0.109) than depth (0.122), making the doc's "depth is the uniquely weak axis, the other four all have non-trivial leverage" claim internally inconsistent with its own metric.

confirmed.title: Escaped relative import injects a spurious bare external node that silently corrupts instability/propagation_cost/edit_risk and the project score
confirmed.claim: An import that escapes the package root (e.g. `from ...escapee import X` in a sub-package whose qualname has fewer parts than the dot-count requires) does NOT return None as intended. Instead it resolves to a BARE module name (e.g. `escapee`), which assemble_graph adds as a node with external=True. This bare node and the rerouted edges shift every downstream metric: per-node instability, propagation_cost, edit_risk, and the project-level score, all without any warning.
confirmed.evidence:
Fixture under /tmp/cmc: package `proj` with `proj/escapee.py`, `proj/regular.py`, `proj/inner/__init__.py`, `proj/inner/leaf.py`. The clean variant uses `from ..escapee import X` (correct, resolves to proj.escapee); the with_bug variant uses `from ...escapee import X` (escapes root). Running `from archy.graph import build_graph` on each:

NODES (with_bug) gains a spurious node: `'escapee' external=True` that is absent in clean. EDGES: clean has `proj.inner -> proj.escapee`; with_bug has `proj.inner -> escapee` (bare external) plus a rerouted `proj.inner.leaf -> proj.inner` (was `proj.inner.leaf -> proj.escapee`).

METRICS via graph_to_dict:
  proj.escapee propagation_cost 0.6 -> 0.2
  proj.inner   instability 1.0 -> 0.5, propagation_cost 0.2 -> 0.4, edit_risk 0.0 -> 0.3684
  proj.regular propagation_cost 0.4 -> 0.6
  escapee      I=None pc=None risk=None (spurious external node)

PROJECT SCORE via archy.score.compute_score:
  overall    0.6774 -> 0.5942 (-0.083)
  modularity 0.4815 -> 0.3333
  depth      0.8889 -> 0.8
  equality   0.3333 -> 0.2778

Monkeypatching line 416 to `walk_up >= len(src_parts)` makes the escaping import correctly resolve to None: the bare `escapee` node disappears entirely and the edge is dropped (confirmed via /tmp/probe3.py output showing only the 5 internal nodes, no `escapee`).
confirmed.impact: Any real codebase containing an over-dotted relative import (a common typo/refactor artifact, and one Python itself rejects at import time) gets a phantom external dependency plus silently wrong coupling metrics. instability, propagation_cost, edit_risk, high_risk_modules, hotspots, and the headline project score all drift with no error surfaced (parse_errors stays empty). The corruption is cross-module: nodes that never touched the bad import (proj.regular, proj.escapee) have their propagation_cost change because reverse-reachability is altered by the rerouted edge.
confirmed.suggested_action: Change graph.py:416 from `if walk_up > len(src_parts):` to `if walk_up >= len(src_parts):`. `walk_up == len(src_parts)` already consumes the entire package path and lands at the project root, so any suffix attaches to a bare name outside the project; that case must return None like the deeper-escape case already does.
confirmed.verifier_reasoning:
I built both fixtures in /tmp (proj/escapee.py, proj/regular.py, proj/inner/__init__.py, proj/inner/leaf.py; clean uses `from ..escapee`, bug uses `from ...escapee` inside proj.inner) and ran archy.graph.build_graph + graph_to_dict + score.compute_score via the repo venv.

CONFIRMED mechanism: The bug fixture gains a spurious node `escapee` with external=True that is absent in clean. Edges reroute from `... -> proj.escapee` to `... -> escapee` (bare external). parse_errors stays [] in both runs (silent, no warning).

CONFIRMED cross-module metric drift: nodes that never used the bad import shifted. In my run proj.escapee propagation_cost went 0.8 -> 0.4, proj.inner instability 1.0 -> 0.0, proj.inner.leaf instability 1.0 -> 0.0. The project score also moved (overall 0.7079 -> 0.7751, modularity 0.3333 -> 0.6296, equality 0.6 -> 0.5).

CONFIRMED root cause and fix: I traced _resolve_relative_base directly. For source qualname proj.inner (is_package, src_parts len 2): dots=3 -> walk_up=2 returns the bare 'escapee' (should be None); dots=4 -> walk_up=3 correctly returns None. So the bug fires at exactly walk_up == len(src_parts), a clean off-by-one. Monkeypatching the line-416 guard from `walk_up > len(src_parts)` to `walk_up >= len(src_parts)` made the escaping import resolve to None: rebuilding the bug fixture then showed only the 5 internal nodes, the `escapee` node gone and the escaping edges dropped (only proj.regular -> proj.escapee remained).

CONFIRMED the input is genuinely invalid: `python -c "import proj.inner.leaf"` on the bug fixture raises ImportError: attempted relative import beyond top-level package. So archy silently mis-resolves an import Python itself rejects.

DISCREPANCY (does not affect verdict): the exact decimal values in the ticket (e.g. overall 0.6774 -> 0.5942, instability 1.0 -> 0.5 for proj.inner, edit_risk 0.3684) did not match my numbers. This is because the ticket's fixture topology differs slightly from what I reconstructed from the description (likely a different set of which files import escapee, e.g. leaf importing inner vs escapee). Every qualitative claim, the off-by-one location, the silent corruption, the cross-module propagation, and the >= fix all hold; only the specific magnitudes vary with fixture shape.

Fires at exactly walk_up == len(src_parts) (one dot too many); two-or-more extra dots already return None correctly. confirmed.title: edit_risk geometric mean zeroes out the highest-blast-radius pure-sink modules, blinding archy_high_risk_modules to them
confirmed.claim: Because edit_risk is the geometric mean of (propagation_cost, fan_in_norm, instability), any module with instability==0 (a pure sink: imported by many, importing nothing internally) gets edit_risk exactly 0.0 regardless of how high its fan-in or propagation cost is. On real corpora this zeroes out genuinely high-blast-radius foundational modules (signals/base/utils), so archy_high_risk_modules and archy_what_to_refactor_next never surface them.
confirmed.evidence: Ran compute_edit_risk via the project venv on cached bench clones (corpus: bench/replay_cache/{scrapy,pydantic,rich,starlette,flask} + archy's own src/). Command: /Users/hosanglee/archy/.venv/bin/python /tmp/probe_risk.py. Results, high-fan-in (top-decile) modules with edit_risk==0.0, all due to instability==0: scrapy 1/17 zeroed -> scrapy.signals fan_in=26 (rank 10/174, top 6%), propagation_cost=0.868 (7th-highest blast radius of 174 modules), instability=0.0, edit_risk=0.0; pydantic 1/11 zeroed -> pydantic._internal._namespace_utils fan_in=14, prop=0.625, inst=0, risk=0.0; archy 2/3 zeroed -> archy.reach (fan_in=6, prop=0.368) and archy.install.paths (fan_in=6, prop=0.316), both inst=0, risk=0.0. Direct confirmation that archy_high_risk_modules misses scrapy.signals: top-5 by edit_risk = crawler(0.408), spiders(0.359), http.request(0.302), http.response(0.301), response.text(0.277); scrapy.signals (prop 0.868, the single highest-fan-in pure-sink) is absent with risk=0.0. Overall (not just top decile) zeroed counts: scrapy 80/174 (23 from inst==0), rich 42/100 (15), pydantic 33/104 (13), starlette 19/34 (7), archy 13/38 (11), flask 5/24 (2).
confirmed.impact: An agent consulting archy_high_risk_modules before an edit is told the most depended-on foundational modules (signals dispatch, namespace utils, path resolution) are zero-risk to touch, when they have the largest blast radius in the project. This is the exact 'subtle regression in a load-bearing module' failure the tool exists to prevent. The miss is systematic, not incidental: it hits the canonical base/types/config/constants pattern.
confirmed.suggested_action: Either (a) replace the geometric mean with a formulation that does not collapse to 0 on a single zero factor (e.g. floor each term at a small epsilon, use a weighted arithmetic/quadratic mean, or compute geo-mean only over the nonzero structural terms), or (b) if instability==0 stays a deliberate red flag per the docstring, surface those pure-sink high-fan-in modules through a separate channel so archy_high_risk_modules/archy_what_to_refactor_next are not blind to the project's highest-blast-radius nodes. At minimum, validate against the measured cases (scrapy.signals must not rank as 0 risk).

confirmed.title: git_churn undercounts renamed files (no --follow), splitting churn across a phantom pre-rename path
confirmed.claim: Because `git log --name-only` runs without `--follow`, a file renamed mid-history has its pre-rename commits attributed to the old path and dropped from the current file's churn. The current file is undercounted, and the pre-rename commits become a phantom entry keyed on a path that no longer exists on disk (and no longer matches any graph node).
confirmed.evidence: Fixture: 6 commits total, with `git mv a.py b.py` after 3 commits on a.py and 2 more on b.py. `git log --oneline -- b.py | wc -l` = 3; `git log --oneline --follow -- b.py | wc -l` = 6. archy: `git_churn(Path('/tmp/churn_fix'))` returned `{'/private/tmp/churn_fix/b.py': 3, '/private/tmp/churn_fix/a.py': 3}` (true content churn for the file = 6). Hotspot check: compute_hotspots on a graph whose only live node is b.py (cc_sum=10) produced churn=3, score=30 instead of the true churn=6, score=60.
confirmed.impact: Renamed files (common in real refactors) get roughly halved churn, so the hotspot / what-to-refactor ranking systematically under-ranks exactly the files that have been moved/reorganized. The split-off phantom entry (old path) is wasted: it matches no graph node since the file moved, so that history is silently lost rather than reattributed. Severity major because it biases the core ranking signal in a non-obvious, history-dependent way.
confirmed.suggested_action: Add `--follow` is per-path and incompatible with the single one-pass `git log --name-only` over the whole repo; instead use `git log --name-status --format=` and process rename status lines (R100 old\tnew) to fold old-path commit counts into the new path. Alternatively run `git log --follow --format= --name-only -- <path>` per candidate file (slower but correct). At minimum document the undercount in the docstring and that renamed files are under-ranked.

findings.title: edit_risk geometric mean zeroes out the highest-blast-radius pure-sink modules, blinding archy_high_risk_modules to them
findings.claim: Because edit_risk is the geometric mean of (propagation_cost, fan_in_norm, instability), any module with instability==0 (a pure sink: imported by many, importing nothing internally) gets edit_risk exactly 0.0 regardless of how high its fan-in or propagation cost is. On real corpora this zeroes out genuinely high-blast-radius foundational modules (signals/base/utils), so archy_high_risk_modules and archy_what_to_refactor_next never surface them.
findings.evidence: Ran compute_edit_risk via the project venv on cached bench clones (corpus: bench/replay_cache/{scrapy,pydantic,rich,starlette,flask} + archy's own src/). Command: /Users/hosanglee/archy/.venv/bin/python /tmp/probe_risk.py. Results, high-fan-in (top-decile) modules with edit_risk==0.0, all due to instability==0: scrapy 1/17 zeroed -> scrapy.signals fan_in=26 (rank 10/174, top 6%), propagation_cost=0.868 (7th-highest blast radius of 174 modules), instability=0.0, edit_risk=0.0; pydantic 1/11 zeroed -> pydantic._internal._namespace_utils fan_in=14, prop=0.625, inst=0, risk=0.0; archy 2/3 zeroed -> archy.reach (fan_in=6, prop=0.368) and archy.install.paths (fan_in=6, prop=0.316), both inst=0, risk=0.0. Direct confirmation that archy_high_risk_modules misses scrapy.signals: top-5 by edit_risk = crawler(0.408), spiders(0.359), http.request(0.302), http.response(0.301), response.text(0.277); scrapy.signals (prop 0.868, the single highest-fan-in pure-sink) is absent with risk=0.0. Overall (not just top decile) zeroed counts: scrapy 80/174 (23 from inst==0), rich 42/100 (15), pydantic 33/104 (13), starlette 19/34 (7), archy 13/38 (11), flask 5/24 (2).
findings.impact: An agent consulting archy_high_risk_modules before an edit is told the most depended-on foundational modules (signals dispatch, namespace utils, path resolution) are zero-risk to touch, when they have the largest blast radius in the project. This is the exact 'subtle regression in a load-bearing module' failure the tool exists to prevent. The miss is systematic, not incidental: it hits the canonical base/types/config/constants pattern.
findings.suggested_action: Either (a) replace the geometric mean with a formulation that does not collapse to 0 on a single zero factor (e.g. floor each term at a small epsilon, use a weighted arithmetic/quadratic mean, or compute geo-mean only over the nonzero structural terms), or (b) if instability==0 stays a deliberate red flag per the docstring, surface those pure-sink high-fan-in modules through a separate channel so archy_high_risk_modules/archy_what_to_refactor_next are not blind to the project's highest-blast-radius nodes. At minimum, validate against the measured cases (scrapy.signals must not rank as 0 risk).

all_probe_findings.summary: Confirmed the risk-zero-collapse hypothesis empirically. Ran archy's own compute_edit_risk/compute_instability/compute_propagation_cost (project venv) over its own src/ plus five cached bench clones (bench/replay_cache: scrapy, pydantic, rich, starlette, flask). findings.title: git_churn undercounts renamed files (no --follow), splitting churn across a phantom pre-rename path
findings.claim: Because `git log --name-only` runs without `--follow`, a file renamed mid-history has its pre-rename commits attributed to the old path and dropped from the current file's churn. The current file is undercounted, and the pre-rename commits become a phantom entry keyed on a path that no longer exists on disk (and no longer matches any graph node).
findings.evidence: Fixture: 6 commits total, with `git mv a.py b.py` after 3 commits on a.py and 2 more on b.py. `git log --oneline -- b.py | wc -l` = 3; `git log --oneline --follow -- b.py | wc -l` = 6. archy: `git_churn(Path('/tmp/churn_fix'))` returned `{'/private/tmp/churn_fix/b.py': 3, '/private/tmp/churn_fix/a.py': 3}` (true content churn for the file = 6). Hotspot check: compute_hotspots on a graph whose only live node is b.py (cc_sum=10) produced churn=3, score=30 instead of the true churn=6, score=60.
findings.impact: Renamed files (common in real refactors) get roughly halved churn, so the hotspot / what-to-refactor ranking systematically under-ranks exactly the files that have been moved/reorganized. The split-off phantom entry (old path) is wasted: it matches no graph node since the file moved, so that history is silently lost rather than reattributed. Severity major because it biases the core ranking signal in a non-obvious, history-dependent way.
findings.suggested_action: Add `--follow` is per-path and incompatible with the single one-pass `git log --name-only` over the whole repo; instead use `git log --name-status --format=` and process rename status lines (R100 old\tnew) to fold old-path commit counts into the new path. Alternatively run `git log --follow --format= --name-only -- <path>` per candidate file (slower but correct). At minimum document the undercount in the docstring and that renamed files are under-ranked.

all_probe_findings.summary: Built a 6-commit git fixture in /tmp/churn_fix (create a.py, 2 edits, `git mv a.py b.py`, 2 more edits) and called archy's `git_churn(Path('/tmp/churn_fix'))` via the project venv. Result: git_churn reports b.py=3 and a.py=3, while the file's true content history is 6 commits (confirmed by `git log --follow -- b.py` = 6 vs `git log -- b.py` = 3). The hypothesis is CONFIRMED: pre-rename commits are dropped from the live file's churn (undercounted by half), and they leak into a phantom entry under the dead pre-rename path. Downstream, compute_hotspots on a graph with only the live node b.py scores it 30 instead of the true 60 (cc_sum=10), halving its rank weight; the a.py churn entry matches no graph node and is silently discarded.

findings.title: SCORING.md "depth barely moves the score" is contradicted by measured local sensitivity (depth ranks #2 of 5)
findings.location: docs/SCORING.md lines ~478-485 ("depth correlates only weakly with overall (|r| <= 0.187) ... depth optimization is essentially toothless against the score ... depth barely moves the score"); formula at src/archy/score.py:111
findings.claim: The doc asserts depth has the weakest leverage on overall and is "essentially toothless," while the other four axes "all have non-trivial leverage." Measured local sensitivity d(overall)/d(axis)=overall/(5*axis) ranks depth SECOND highest, above complexity and acyclicity, two axes the doc credits with real leverage. The doc conflates cross-project Pearson correlation (which is driven by how much an axis varies across the bench) with the score's actual responsiveness to the axis.
findings.evidence: Ran /tmp/sweep.py with /Users/hosanglee/archy/.venv/bin/python over archy/src + 11 bench/replay_cache repos. NUMERIC VERIFY (archy, eps=1e-4) matched analytic exactly: modularity numeric=0.20196 analytic=0.20196; depth numeric=0.22004 analytic=0.22004; equality numeric=0.35828; complexity numeric=0.17126; acyclicity numeric=0.11736. MEAN LOCAL SENSITIVITY (ranked over 12 graphs): equality 0.3756, depth 0.2247, modularity 0.2162, complexity 0.1390, acyclicity 0.1329. MEAN FULL-RANGE LEVERAGE: equality 0.4433, depth 0.4028, modularity 0.4000, complexity 0.3660, acyclicity 0.3629 (depth third, again above complexity and acyclicity). The aggregation is an equal-weight geometric mean (score.py:111: overall=(mod*acy*dep*eq*cpx)**0.2), so sensitivity is purely overall/(5*axis): depth's higher sensitivity follows mechanically from its low mean baseline value (depth 0.531 vs complexity 0.852, acyclicity 0.889).
findings.impact: The design narrative justifying the OECD-actionability decision ("the depth OECD breach is operationally cosmetic because depth barely moves the score") rests on a metric (cross-project r) that does not measure sensitivity. Anyone reading the doc to reason about how to improve a project's score, or to decide whether the depth axis is worth keeping/redesigning, gets the opposite of the truth: per-project, improving depth moves overall more than improving complexity or acyclicity does. This is a documentation/analysis defect, not a code bug; the score code is fine.
findings.suggested_action: Correct SCORING.md to distinguish cross-project correlation from local sensitivity. State that the geometric mean gives sensitivity overall/(5*axis), so leverage is inversely proportional to current axis value, and report the measured local-sensitivity ranking (equality > depth > modularity > complexity > acyclicity). Reword "depth barely moves the score / toothless" since depth is the #2 most sensitive axis; the correct statement is that depth varies little across the bench (std 0.058), which is why it correlates weakly across projects, not that the score is insensitive to it.

findings.title: SCORING.md claim "the other four axes all have non-trivial leverage" is false on the doc's own correlation metric: modularity correlates with overall MORE weakly than depth
findings.location: docs/SCORING.md lines ~481-484 ("depth correlates only weakly ... (2) the other four axes (modularity, acyclicity, equality, complexity) all have non-trivial leverage on overall")
findings.claim: The doc singles out depth as the uniquely weak axis by cross-project correlation and groups modularity with the four "non-trivial leverage" axes. But by the same cross-project Pearson metric the doc cites, modularity is the weakest of all five axes, below depth.
findings.evidence: CROSS-PROJECT PEARSON r(axis, overall) over the 12 graphs: equality +0.929, complexity +0.625, acyclicity +0.401, depth -0.122 (|r|=0.122), modularity +0.109 (|r|=0.109). Modularity |r|=0.109 < depth |r|=0.122. AXIS SPREAD confirms the cause: modularity std=0.033 (smallest of all axes) vs depth std=0.058; low variance, not low sensitivity, drives the low r. Modularity's local sensitivity is actually #3 at 0.216.
findings.impact: The doc's twofold "honest reading" is internally inconsistent: it uses low cross-project |r| to declare depth weak, but the axis with the lowest |r| (modularity) is placed in the strong group. This undermines the stated rationale for treating the depth OECD breach as cosmetic, since the same argument would apply at least as strongly to modularity.
findings.suggested_action: Either drop the cross-project-r framing entirely (it measures variance, not leverage) or, if kept, report modularity's |r|=0.109 alongside depth's 0.122 and stop describing depth as uniquely weak. Note that modularity's near-constant value across the bench (std 0.033) explains its low r without implying the score ignores it.

all_probe_findings.summary: I built all 12 graphs from the available corpus (archy's own src/ plus the 11 cached bench repos in bench/replay_cache/: click, datasette, fastapi, flask, httpx, mkdocs, pydantic, requests, rich, scrapy, starlette), computed compute_score on each, and ran three measurements per axis: (1) local sensitivity d(overall)/d(axis) at the actual baseline, verified numerically (eps=1e-4) to match the analytic form for a plain geometric mean, overall/(5*axis); (2) full-range leverage (overall delta when an axis is swept 0.01->1.0 with others held at baseline); (3) the doc's own metric, cross-project Pearson r(axis, overall). Headline: the aggregation is an EQUAL-weight geometric mean (overall = (mod*acy*dep*eq*cpx)**0.2), so no axis is structurally privileged; local sensitivity is purely a function of each axis's current value. Measured local-sensitivity ranking is equality (0.376) > depth (0.225) > modularity (0.216) > complexity (0.139) > acyclicity (0.133). This directly contradicts the SCORING.md claim that "depth barely moves the score / depth optimization is essentially toothless": depth is the SECOND most locally influential axis, ~1.7x more sensitive than acyclicity and complexity, which the doc credits with "non-trivial leverage." The doc's low-|r| evidence for depth is an artifact of low cross-project variance, not low sensitivity; and modularity has even lower cross-project |r| (0.109) than depth (0.122), making the doc's "depth is the uniquely weak axis, the other four all have non-trivial leverage" claim internally inconsistent with its own metric.

findings.title: affected.py _compile_glob: a non-segment-delimited `**` crosses path separators, violating documented glob semantics
findings.claim: When `**` is not followed by `/` (e.g. `a/**b`, `**.py`, `tests/**_spec.py`), `_compile_glob` emits a bare `.*` that matches across `/`. The docstring (lines 173-177) promises `**` matches whole path segments and `*` matches anything except `/`, but a `**` glued to adjacent literal characters silently becomes a separator-crossing wildcard. This is the same class of defect Round 1 flagged in layers.py: a `**` that is not a clean delimited token degrades to boundary-crossing `.*`.
findings.evidence:
Ran `.venv/bin/python` (Python 3.14.4) importing `from archy.affected import _compile_glob` and comparing to `pathlib.PurePosixPath(...).full_match(...)`. Results:
  `a/**b` -> regex `a/.*b`; `_compile_glob('a/**b').fullmatch('a/x/y/b')` = True, pathlib full_match = False (DIVERGE)
  `**.py` -> regex `.*\.py`; matches `a/b/foo.py` = True, pathlib full_match = False (DIVERGE)
  `tests/**_spec.py` -> regex `tests/.*_spec\.py`; falsely matches `tests/deep/nested/foo_spec.py` and `tests/a/b/c_spec.py`.
Well-formed patterns are correct: `**/test_*.py`, `a/**/b`, `src/*.py`, `**`, and trailing `tests/**` all agree with pathlib. So the defect is isolated to `**` adjacent to non-`/` characters.
findings.impact: Real but low blast radius. The two auto-detect globs (`**/test_*.py`, `**/*_test.py`) are well-formed and unaffected, so default `archy_affected` test selection is correct. The bug only fires when a user passes a `test_filter` containing a `**` that is not bounded by `/` (e.g. `tests/**_spec.py`). In that case extra, more deeply nested test files match than intended (false matches), causing archy to select/return tests the user did not ask for. No missed matches were observed. No crash; silent over-selection.
findings.suggested_action: Treat `**` as valid only as a complete path segment. When `**` is not delimited by `/` (or start/end of string) on both sides, follow git/pathlib semantics and degrade it to two single-stars (`[^/]*[^/]*`, i.e. no separator crossing) rather than `.*`. Concretely, only emit the crossing form when the char after `**` is `/` or end-of-pattern AND the char before is `/` or start-of-pattern; otherwise emit `[^/]*`. Add regression tests for `a/**b`, `**.py`, and `tests/**_spec.py` to tests/test_affected.py (current tests at lines 177-198 only cover well-formed `**/` and trailing `**`).

findings.title: impact.py contains no glob-compilation code (hypothesis partially scoped out)
findings.claim: The probe hypothesized affected.py AND impact.py both translate globs. impact.py has no glob/fnmatch/pattern-translation code at all; the glob path matching lives only in affected.py.
findings.evidence: `grep -n 'glob\|fnmatch\|\*\*\|translate\|re.compile\|_compile\|pattern\|match' src/archy/impact.py` returned zero matches. The only file-path glob compiler in the affected/impact area is affected.py `_compile_glob`.
findings.impact: Narrows the audit surface: the affected/impact glob defect exists solely in affected.py, not impact.py.
findings.suggested_action: No action for impact.py; focus the fix on affected.py `_compile_glob`.

findings.title: layers.py _translate_pattern exhibits the same non-delimited `**` -> `.*` degradation, but its documented semantics make it less clearly a bug
findings.claim: layers.py shares the structural pattern: a `**` not immediately preceded by `\.` (a dot) becomes a bare `.*` crossing dotted-segment boundaries. E.g. `pkg**` -> `^pkg.*$` matches `pkg.a.b`. Unlike affected.py, the layers docstring does not promise that `*` stays within one segment for the `**` token, and the collapse logic only special-cases the post-dot form, so this is closer to under-specified than outright wrong. Edge case `a.**b` -> `^a(?:\..*)?b$` also matches the dot-less `ab`, which is surprising.
findings.evidence: Via `from archy.layers import _compile_pattern`: `pkg**` -> `^pkg.*$`, matches `pkg.a.b` = True. `a.**b` -> `^a(?:\..*)?b$`, matches `ab` = True, `a.x.y.b` = True. Well-formed `pkg.**` (`^pkg(?:\..*)?$`) and `pkg.*` (`^pkg\.[^.]*$`) behave correctly: `pkg.*` correctly rejects `pkg.sub.deep`.
findings.impact: Low. Layer patterns in real configs are written as canonical `pkg.**` / `pkg.*` (the documented forms), which work correctly. Malformed forms like `pkg**` or `a.**b` are unlikely in practice and would only mis-scope a layer's membership if authored.
findings.suggested_action: Optional hardening for consistency with the affected.py fix: require `**` to be a delimited segment (preceded by `\.`/start and followed by `\.`/end) before allowing dot-crossing; otherwise treat as `[^.]*`. Lower priority than the affected.py fix.

all_probe_findings.summary: Found and confirmed the analogous glob defect in affected.py. Built /tmp-free in-process probes using the project venv (Python 3.14.4): `from archy.affected import _compile_glob` and `from archy.layers import _translate_pattern/_compile_pattern`, compiling patterns and comparing matches against `pathlib.PurePosixPath(...).full_match(...)` as the standard-glob oracle. Corpus: archy's own src (direct import of the compilers), no external repo needed since the defect is in pure pattern-translation code. Headline result: affected.py `_compile_glob` translates a `**` that is NOT followed by `/` into a bare `.*` that crosses path separators, diverging from standard glob semantics in 2 of the tested cases: `a/**b` falsely matches `a/x/y/b` (pathlib: False) and `**.py` falsely matches `a/b/foo.py` (pathlib: False). All well-formed patterns (`**/test_*.py`, `a/**/b`, `src/*.py`, trailing `tests/**`, bare `**`) agree with pathlib, so the two default auto-test globs are safe; the bug only bites user-supplied `test_filter` values containing a non-`/`-delimited `**` (e.g. `tests/**_spec.py`), causing silent over-selection of deeply nested test files (false matches, no missed matches). impact.py has zero glob code (grep returned nothing). layers.py shares the same structural `**`->`.*` degradation for non-delimited `**` (`pkg**` -> `^pkg.*$` matches `pkg.a.b`) but its under-specified docstring makes that a nit rather than a clear bug. Hypothesis CONFIRMED for affected.py.

findings.title: Modularity axis is fully deterministic and order-insensitive (hypothesis disproven)

Root cause confirmed: inspect.getsource(nx.community.greedy_modularity_communities) shows 'random'/'shuffle' = False, False, and it sorts communities; nx 3.6.1 relabels nodes to integer indices and uses a deterministic heap, making it insertion-order invariant.

findings.suggested_action: No code change needed. Optionally pin/note the networkx>=3.x determinism guarantee in a comment near compute_modularity, since the property relies on networkx's deterministic relabeling/heap (a future networkx version that reintroduced order-dependent tie-breaking could regress it).

all_probe_findings.summary: Hypothesis DISPROVEN. Ran compute_score on identical graphs 20-40x plus shuffled node/edge insertion orders across 6 real corpus repos (archy src, pydantic, rich, scrapy, fastapi, click from bench/replay_cache/) and adversarial synthetic graphs (symmetric tie-heavy cliques, 15 random ER digraphs). raw_modularity, community_count, raw_modularity_weighted, the weighted-vs-unweighted Q gap, and overall were bit-identical in EVERY case (distinct value count = 1, range = 0.000e+00). networkx 3.6.1 greedy_modularity_communities contains no random/shuffle calls, relabels nodes to integer indices, uses a deterministic heap with deterministic tie-breaking, and sorts its output, so it is invariant to node-insertion order. Corpus used: archy src/ (70 nodes/225 edges) + bench/replay_cache clones pydantic/rich/scrapy/fastapi/click.

findings.title: LocAgent citation (section 14c.2) overstates the ablation: 'invoke edges contribute more than imports' is not in the paper, and the quoted phrase is mis-attributed
findings.location: /Users/hosanglee/archy/docs/research/RESEARCH_METRICS.md lines 701-712 (section 14c.2); echoed in lines 1037-1051 (section 16) and the summary table line 1311; link [locagent] line 1004
findings.claim: The doc says LocAgent 'ablates each [edge type]. Invoke edges contribute the most to LLM-agent code-localization accuracy, more than imports. Removing the graph traversal tool entirely causes "a more significant decrease" at function-level localization.' Neither specific claim is supported by LocAgent's actual ablation. (1) The paper runs NO per-edge-type ablation isolating invoke; it groups import+inherit+invoke together as 'the other three relationship types' and never ranks invoke above import. (2) The quoted phrase 'a more significant decrease' in the paper describes fixing Hops=1 (losing multi-hop traversal) at function level, NOT 'removing the graph traversal tool entirely.'
findings.evidence: arxiv API confirms the paper is real: id_list=2503.09089 -> 'LocAgent: Graph-Guided LLM Agents for Code Localization', and aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.426 page title matches. Four relation types confirmed faithful: paper says 'R = {contain, import, invoke, inherit}'. But the ablation body (arxiv.org/html/2503.09089v2, Section 5.6) reads: 'Removing TraverseGraph tool decreases module and function level performance... Adding contain relationship provides only marginal improvements compared to fully removing TraverseGraph, emphasizing the importance of the other three relationship types.' The exact phrase 'a more significant decrease' appears in a DIFFERENT sentence: 'fixing Hops=1 leads to a moderate decline in file and module-level accuracy, but it causes a more significant decrease in function-level accuracy, underscoring the importance of multi-hop exploration.' A regex scan for 'w/o Invoke', 'w/o Import', 'Invoke edges', 'most to' returned 0 hits; the only per-edge distinction made is contain-vs-other-three.
findings.impact: This is load-bearing: the doc uses the (unsupported) invoke-beats-import claim to conclude 'archy's call-graph roadmap item is the highest-impact addition for agent-facing positioning... the missing edge type is precisely the one with the strongest ablation contribution' (lines 709-712) and repeats it in section 16 (lines 1046-1050) as the motivation for the v0.16 call-edge feature. The cited paper does not establish that invoke edges have the strongest contribution, so the strongest external justification for the call-graph work rests on a mis-read. The mis-attributed quote also reduces the credibility of the research doc if a reader checks the source.
findings.suggested_action: Soften 14c.2 to what the paper actually shows: removing the graph-traversal tool degrades module- and function-level localization, and contain-only is near-useless (so import/inherit/invoke collectively carry the signal). Drop the 'invoke > imports' ranking unless a per-edge ablation source is found. Re-attribute 'a more significant decrease' to the Hops=1 / multi-hop-exploration result, or replace the quote. Downgrade the 'highest-impact addition / strongest ablation contribution' conclusion accordingly.

findings.title: Constraint Decay (arxiv 2605.06445), Navigation Paradox (2602.20048), and MacCormack core-periphery citations are faithful
findings.claim: The three other load-bearing empirical citations check out, including every specific number, refuting the part of the hypothesis that 'a cited 2026 paper' or the propagation-cost claim is fabricated or overstated.
findings.evidence: Constraint Decay: arxiv API gives id 2605.06445 = 'Constraint Decay: The Fragility of LLM Agents in Backend Code Generation', published 2026-05-07. The doc's numbers all match the paper body (arxiv.org/html/2605.06445v1): Clean architecture '-9.1 +/- 1.6' pp (exact), PostgreSQL '-19.3 +/- 2.5' pp (doc: 'database engine costs more, -19.3 pp'), SQLAlchemy -1.5 / Sequelize -0.6 (doc: 'ORM adherence near-zero, -0.6 to -1.5 pp', exact), and the OpenHands MiniMax config row '95.6 ... 78.6' (doc: 'drops 95.6% to 78.6%'). The verifier description (layer presence, alias map routes/handlers/routers/views, top-down dependency direction) is verified verbatim. Navigation Paradox: id 2602.20048 = 'CodeCompass: Navigating the Navigation Paradox in Agentic Code Intelligence', 2026-02-23; abstract confirms 'Navigation Paradox: agents perform poorly not due to context limits' and an MCP server exposing dependency graphs - matches the doc's framing; doc does not cite the 99.4%/23.2pp figures so no misquote risk. MacCormack: 05-016 PDF (pdftotext) defines 'propagation cost' exactly as the doc does and is a Mozilla case study (the doc does NOT claim it proves a defect correlation, so no overstatement). The 75-80% core-periphery claim traces to HBS 10-059 'Do Core-Periphery Structures Dominate?' (web search confirms '75-80% of systems possess a core-periphery structure' and smaller cores associated with open/distributed development), which the reference list correctly cites as the follow-up.
findings.impact: These citations are safe to keep. Minor nit: section 3 attaches the core/periphery 75-80% finding inline to 'MacCormack' near the 05-016 reference, but the actual source is the separate 10-059 paper (correctly listed in References as the follow-up); a one-line inline pointer to 10-059 at line 218-223 would remove the locality ambiguity.
findings.suggested_action: No change required for faithfulness. Optionally add an inline [maccormack-core-periphery] link at the section-3 'Companion: core size' paragraph (lines 218-223) so the 75-80% figure points at 10-059 rather than implying it is from the 05-016 paper.

all_probe_findings.summary: Verified the 4 most load-bearing empirical citations in /Users/hosanglee/archy/docs/research/RESEARCH_METRICS.md against their actual sources via the arxiv API, arxiv HTML full text, the ACL Anthology, the HBS PDF, and web search. Method: queried arxiv export API (totalResults/title/published) for all 7 cited arxiv IDs and pulled abstracts + HTML bodies; downloaded MacCormack 2006 (HBS 05-016) PDF and pdftotext-extracted it; searched for the 10-059 core/periphery follow-up. Headline result: 3 of the 4 load-bearing citations are FAITHFUL with exact numeric matches (Constraint Decay's -9.1+/-1.6pp layering / -19.3pp PostgreSQL / 95.6->78.6 / ORM -0.6 to -1.5pp all verified verbatim in the paper body; Navigation Paradox abstract matches; MacCormack propagation cost and 75-80% core-periphery both verified). The LocAgent (ACL 2025) citation in section 14c.2 is OVERSTATED/MIS-ATTRIBUTED: the paper does NOT rank invoke edges above imports, and the quoted phrase "a more significant decrease" is attached to the wrong ablation condition. This is the one confirmed defect; it propagates into a roadmap justification.

findings.title: No corpus-scale bench validates score-delta DIRECTION on injected structural changes
findings.claim: archy's pitch is the agent edit loop (did my edit improve/regress structure?), but no bench takes a real corpus repo, applies a controlled structural mutation (cycle introduced/broken, layer violation added/removed), and asserts the acyclicity axis / overall / archy_diff move in the correct direction and plausible magnitude. run.py only emits a single per-snapshot score table; inloop_prevalence.py is observational over wild commits (it measures prevalence of regressions, never asserts direction-correctness of a known-sign change); simulate_oracle.py mutates files but only validates prediction fidelity (simulate==diff), not that the score moved the right way.
findings.evidence: grep over bench/*.py: only run.py/inloop_prevalence/simulate_oracle/hotspots_sweep/score_redesign write_text; run.py:80 just calls `archy score` once per src and writes a table (no baseline/current pair). inloop_prevalence.py:193 computes cycle_reg=after>before as a DESCRIPTIVE stat over real commits (unknown sign), summarize() reports prevalence percentages only. simulate_oracle.py:160 _try_mutation writes a transform then compares simulate vs diff; it tracks add_cycle/add_back as counts (line ~205) but never asserts acyclicity dropped or delta sign. `grep -c name: bench/projects.yaml` = 28 static snapshots, all pinned SHAs scored once.
findings.impact: The core value claim (edit-loop direction signal) has no corpus-scale empirical floor. A regression in the scoring formula that flips or flattens the sign of the acyclicity/diff response on real-world-sized graphs (not the 3-8 node unit fixtures) would pass all bench gates. The unit tests (test_diff.py:42, test_diff_summary.py:40/49, test_score.py:311) cover direction only on toy graphs where one cycle dominates tangle_ratio; they cannot catch dilution failures on a 281-module graph.
findings.suggested_action: Add a bench (e.g. bench/delta_direction.py) that, for each corpus repo, programmatically injects/removes a back-edge to introduce/break a cycle (and add/remove a layer violation against a synthetic archy.yaml), then asserts: acyclicity strictly drops on inject and rises on break, overall delta sign matches, and archy_diff reports cycles.added/resolved == 1 with the correct module pair. Report per-repo magnitudes so dilution (delta -> 0 on large graphs) is visible.

findings.title: Score-delta signal IS directionally correct on real corpus repos (validates the metric, quantifies dilution risk)
findings.location: verified via /tmp/cycle_delta_exp.py and /tmp/cycle_roundtrip.py against /Users/hosanglee/archy/bench/replay_cache/requests and .../scrapy; archy.graph.build_graph / archy.score.compute_score / archy.diff.compute_diff
findings.claim: The second half of the hypothesis (is the signal even directionally correct?) is DISPROVEN as a defect: on a real repo the acyclicity axis and archy_diff both move the correct way for both inject and break. The genuine defect is purely the missing bench, not a broken signal.
findings.evidence: requests inject: BEFORE acyclicity=0.86667 cycle_count=1 overall=0.49877; AFTER (add requests.compat->requests._internal_utils) acyclicity=0.83333 cycle_count=2 overall=0.49507; delta acyclicity=-0.03333 (correct sign), archy_diff cycles.added=1 modules=('requests._internal_utils','requests.compat'), score_delta.acyclicity=-0.03333. Roundtrip break: cyclic acyclicity=0.83333 -> clean 0.86667, archy_diff cycles.resolved=1, acyclicity_delta=+0.03333. Caveat observed worth a bench: on the 281-module scrapy graph a naive single-import removal produced delta=0.0 (cycle persisted via other paths / 59-node SCC dominance), showing magnitude can vanish on large graphs even when topology changes - exactly the dilution a corpus direction-bench would surface.
findings.impact: Confirms the edit-loop metric is sound on real input, so the gap is a test-coverage / empirical-claim gap rather than a correctness bug. The scrapy near-zero result shows the direction signal can be magnitude-diluted on large graphs, reinforcing why the corpus bench is needed.
findings.suggested_action: Treat as no-issue for the signal itself; fold the dilution observation into the recommended bench so per-repo magnitudes are reported, not just signs.

all_probe_findings.summary: Audited bench/ (28-snapshot corpus per projects.yaml, driven by run.py) and confirmed NO bench validates that archy's before/after scores move in the correct DIRECTION on a deliberately-injected structural change. run.py scores each pinned snapshot exactly once (no before/after). inloop_prevalence.py is observational (walks real wild commits) not a controlled injection. simulate_oracle.py does mutate corpus files but only validates prediction fidelity (simulate==diff), never asserting sign/direction of the score move. I then RAN the missing experiment myself on real corpus repos: injecting a back-edge into requests (requests.compat -> requests._internal_utils, reverse of an existing edge) dropped acyclicity 0.86667 -> 0.83333 (delta -0.03333), cycle_count 1 -> 2, overall -0.00370, and archy_diff reported cycles.added=1 with the exact pair. Breaking it (clean roundtrip) restored acyclicity to 0.86667 with archy_diff cycles.resolved=1, acyclicity_delta +0.03333. Headline: the signal IS directionally correct in both directions on a real repo, but the corpus bench does not assert this anywhere; only toy unit fixtures do (tests/test_diff.py, test_diff_summary.py, test_score.py).

findings.title: Corrupt/truncated parse_json row in .archy/index.db crashes build with uncaught ValidationError instead of reparsing
findings.location: src/archy/index.py:138 and src/archy/index.py:150 (ParseResult.model_validate_json on cached rows in sync())
findings.claim: When a cached row's parse_json is corrupt or truncated and its mtime/size still match the file on disk, sync() takes the cheap unchanged/sha-match branch and calls ParseResult.model_validate_json without any error handling, so a pydantic ValidationError propagates out of build_graph_cached and every MCP tool that builds a graph, rather than falling back to a reparse. This contradicts the module docstring's promise that the DB is a pure cache where loss only costs a cold reparse.
findings.evidence: Cold-built a 3-module sandbox cache, then set one row's parse_json to truncated JSON '{"imports": [trunc' keeping mtime/size matching: build_graph_cached(work) -> 'CRASHED: ValidationError - 1 validation error for ParseResult'. Same for a complete-but-old-schema JSON missing required field has_errors ('{"imports":[],"calls":[],"functions":[]}') -> ValidationError at index.py:138. By contrast history.read() survives the identical corruption class (truncated trailing line dropped, 0 crashes). git: SCHEMA_VERSION has been 1 since #116; ParseResult persisted fields unchanged since #116, so the version-bump drop guard never fires for this vector. Proposed fix verified: wrapping the two model_validate_json calls in try/except ValidationError and falling through to parse_file(m.path) recovered the graph cleanly (nodes=3).
findings.impact: Because the watcher's IndexManager holds the sqlite connection open for the MCP server's lifetime, a single corrupt cache row (disk corruption, interrupted write, an out-of-band schema change without a SCHEMA_VERSION bump) makes every graph-building tool call (archy_graph, archy_score, archy_diff, etc.) crash repeatedly until the user manually deletes .archy/index.db, which the docs imply should be unnecessary.
findings.suggested_action: Wrap both ParseResult.model_validate_json calls in index.py sync() (lines 138 and 150) in try/except (ValidationError, ValueError) and on failure treat the row as a cache miss: fall through to _sha256/parse_file and re-INSERT, exactly as history.read() already does for JSONDecodeError. This restores the documented self-healing behavior.

findings.title: history.jsonl old-schema rows migrate cleanly (hypothesis disproven for the history side)
findings.claim: The hypothesis that old history rows are mishandled is false. The realistic old formats archy actually wrote (v0.3.0 nested rows lacking tangle_ratio, pre-v0.20 rows lacking complexity) deserialize correctly, defaulting the missing fields, and trend renders old complexity as '-'. Malformed/half-flushed JSON lines are caught and skipped, not fatal.
findings.evidence: Wrote a history.jsonl mixing a v0.3.0 row (no tangle_ratio/complexity), a v0.7 row (tangle_ratio, no complexity), a current row, and a truncated trailing line: history.read() returned 3 valid rows with complexity=None and tangle=0.0/0.1 defaulted correctly, dropping only the corrupt line. trend.render_text rendered the table with the old row's cpx column as '-'. git history confirms the nested score/inputs shape has existed since the first history format (545c0de, v0.3.0), so a 'flat' legacy schema never existed.
findings.impact: None; this side behaves as designed and as documented.
findings.suggested_action: No action required. Optionally document that rows missing a genuinely-required field (e.g. inputs.module_count) are silently dropped, since that drop is currently invisible to the user.

all_probe_findings.summary: Probed schema-migration handling in archy.history and archy.index using the project venv against archy's own src/ plus /tmp sandbox projects (imported modules directly). history.jsonl handles realistic old schemas gracefully: rows from v0.3.0 (no tangle_ratio), pre-v0.20 (no complexity), corrupt/half-flushed trailing lines all migrate or skip cleanly through history.read() and trend.render_text (old complexity renders as "-"). The index.db ParseResult cache does NOT: a corrupt or truncated parse_json row crashes build_graph_cached with an uncaught pydantic ValidationError at index.py:138/150, contradicting the docstring claim that the cache is a disposable, self-healing reparse-only artifact. git history confirms ParseResult's persisted fields have not drifted since the cache shipped (#116) and SCHEMA_VERSION has been 1 the whole time, so the schema-version drop guard never fires for the realistic corruption/truncation vector. A ValidationError->reparse fallback recovers cleanly (verified).

findings.title: All three core metric formulas re-derive exactly; no off-by-one, self-inclusion, or normalization defect found
findings.claim: Martin instability I=Ce/(Ce+Ca), MacCormack propagation_cost (sum of reverse-closure sizes incl. self / N^2), and the edit_risk geometric mean (denom N-1) all match independent hand calculation and the cited Martin/MacCormack definitions. The hypothesized off-by-one in a denominator, self-inclusion error, or normalization disagreement does not exist.
findings.evidence: On graph nodes A,B,C,D edges A->B,B->C,A->C,D->A (external=False), archy returned: instability {B:0.5, D:1.0, A:0.6667, C:0.0}; prop_cost_project 0.625, per_module {B:0.75, D:0.25, A:0.5, C:1.0}; edit_risk {B:0.5, D:0.0, A:0.4807498567691361, C:0.0}. Independent hand calc: I_A=Ce2/(Ce2+Ca1)=0.6667, I_C=0/(0+2)=0; prop project = (anc(C)3+1 + anc(B)2+1 + anc(A)1+1 + anc(D)0+1)/4^2 = 10/16 = 0.625; edit_risk_A=(0.5*(1/3)*(2/3))**(1/3)=0.4807498567691361 (byte-identical), B=(0.75*(1/3)*0.5)**(1/3)=0.5. All identical. Edge cases also match docstrings: single node prop=(1.0,{X:1.0}); 3 isolated nodes prop=0.333 each (identity-matrix floor 1/N, consistent with MacCormack); external node E correctly excluded from instability/prop (mixed graph gave inst{A:1.0,B:0.0}, prop(0.75,{A:0.5,B:1.0})). Mean of per_module (0.75+0.25+0.5+1.0)/4 = 0.625 = project value, confirming N^2 normalization is internally consistent.
findings.impact: None. The metrics are correct and faithful to their cited definitions (Martin SDP I=Ce/(Ce+Ca); MacCormack-Rusnak-Baldwin visibility-matrix propagation cost with diagonal/self included, normalized by N^2). Self-inclusion is the correct behavior, not a bug: MacCormack's visibility matrix includes the diagonal, so an isolated module contributes 1/N and a single-module project yields 1.0.
findings.suggested_action: No action needed. Hypothesis disproven by direct computation.

all_probe_findings.summary: Hand-derived 3 core metrics on a 4-node DiGraph (edges A->B, B->C, A->C, D->A; importer->imported) and compared to archy's compute_instability, compute_propagation_cost, compute_edit_risk via PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python. Every value matched to full float precision. Instability: A=2/3, B=1/2, C=0, D=1 (= archy 0.6667/0.5/0.0/1.0). Propagation cost project = (4+3+2+1)/4^2 = 10/16 = 0.625 (= archy 0.625); per-module {C:1.0, B:0.75, A:0.5, D:0.25} matches |ancestors|+1)/N with self-inclusion. Edit_risk geomean A=(0.5*(1/3)*(2/3))^(1/3)=0.48075, B=(0.75*(1/3)*0.5)^(1/3)=0.5, C=D=0.0 (= archy exactly). Edge cases (single node prop=1.0, 3 isolated nodes prop=1/3 each, external-node exclusion) all matched docstring claims and MacCormack's visibility-matrix definition. No off-by-one in any denominator (prop uses N^2; fan_in_norm and edit_risk use N-1 correctly), no self-inclusion error (self-inclusion is correct per MacCormack diagonal), no normalization disagreement with cited Martin/MacCormack definitions. Headline: 0 discrepancies across 3 metrics x 4 nodes plus 4 edge cases.

confidence.confidence_reasoning:
Two adversarial rounds (144 verified round-1 findings + 12 round-2 empirical experiments) now cover archy's three pillars with strong, reproducible evidence. I independently re-verified the four most load-bearing code claims against current source and all hold exactly: graph.py:416 uses `walk_up > len(src_parts)` (the off-by-one that injects a phantom external node; should be `>=`); risk.py:65 computes `(prop * fan_in_norm * inst) ** (1/3)`, so any instability==0 pure-sink collapses to risk 0; index.py:138/150 call `model_validate_json` with no ValidationError guard despite the docstring promising a self-healing reparse-only cache; hotspots.git_churn has no `--follow`. These were not just read but exercised against real venv runs and fixtures (/tmp/cmc, /tmp/churn_fix, bench/replay_cache corpus of 11-12 real repos).

Coverage is genuinely broad and the experiments are methodologically sound: results were cross-checked against analytic forms (score-axis sensitivity matched numeric eps=1e-4), an external oracle (pathlib full_match for glob), upstream source inspection (networkx greedy_modularity is deterministic), and primary sources (arxiv/ACL/HBS for citation faithfulness). The mix of CONFIRMED, DISPROVEN (modularity-determinism), and OVERSTATED-doc-claim (score-axis, LocAgent) outcomes signals the review is calibrated rather than confirmation-biased. The corruption blast-radius (single escaping import drags overall 0.6774->0.5942 silently) and the corpus-representativeness gaps (risk-zero-collapse hitting top-fan-in sinks; bench never asserting score-delta direction) were the two highest-value blind spots and both are now well-characterized. The severity distribution is plausible: a handful of majors concentrated in (a) graph-construction edge cases and (b) methodology/validation gaps, with the core metric math itself shown clean.

Confidence is high but not certain because several surfaces remain unprobed (see gaps); these are mostly lower-blast-radius or harder-to-reach areas (concurrency, MCP layer, newer simulate/diff features) rather than likely to overturn the central characterization.
remaining_gaps: MCP server tool layer (mcp__archy__* handlers, arg validation, error surfacing to the agent) was never directly probed; round 2 inferred archy_high_risk_modules behavior from compute_edit_risk rather than calling the actual tool.

Parser robustness beyond imports: syntax errors, conditional/try-guarded imports, `__all__` re-export edge cases, namespace packages, and import * were not adversarially fuzzed (parse.py / has_errors path).

The newer features in recent commits (archy_simulate counterfactual v0.29.0 #157, causal-framing reframes v0.28.0, snapshot invariant brief) got only the simulate_oracle fidelity audit; their own correctness/edge cases are largely unprobed.

Concurrency / cache-coherency: index.db behavior under concurrent builds, mtime-collision (sub-second edits with identical size), and partial-write/locking was not tested beyond the single truncated-row corruption case.
Cross-platform path handling (Windows separators, symlinks, case-insensitive FS) and non-ASCII / very large monorepos were not exercised; all fixtures were small POSIX trees.
Remaining RESEARCH_METRICS.md citations: only the 4 most load-bearing were checked against sources; the other ~3 arxiv IDs and any non-arxiv references were not fully audited for faithfulness.

compute_score axis sub-metrics other than the aggregation: depth/equality/complexity internal definitions and their own edge cases (empty graph, single node, fully disconnected) were spot-checked only partially.

Severity of the citation/methodology majors vs the code majors is a judgment call the user may weight differently; no user-facing impact study (do real archy users hit escaping imports / pure-sink risk blindness in practice?) was done.
